analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set legal limits on PFAS pollution discharged into water by major industries.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would force EPA to set PFAS discharge limits for eight industries by 2028 and put up $200 million a year to help sewage plants handle the chemicals, has sat untouched in committee since it was introduced in December 2025 with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the EPA to write federal water pollution limits for PFAS — the "forever chemicals" linked to cancer and other health problems — for industries that discharge them, including plastics, metal plating, textile mills, and landfills, with firm deadlines between 2026 and 2028. It would also immediately require those industries to start monitoring and reporting their PFAS discharges, and it would give $200 million a year to publicly owned sewage treatment plants so they can filter PFAS out of the water they handle. It has not moved since Senator Gillibrand introduced it.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from, fish in, or live near waterways receiving industrial PFAS discharges would get enforceable limits on the chemicals entering their water, and families whose water is treated at public sewage plants would benefit from the $200 million-a-year grants that help those plants screen and filter PFAS. Communities downstream of plastics plants, plating shops, textile mills, and landfills gain the most, since those industries would face the first hard deadlines.

how_it_helps.text: Within three years, EPA would have to publish federal human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS chemical and class, creating a scientific baseline for how much PFAS is safe in the water people use.

EPA would have to finalize enforceable discharge limits (effluent limitations guidelines) for specific industries on a set schedule: organic chemicals and plastics, electroplating, and metal finishing by September 2026; textile mills and landfills by September 2027; leather tanning, paint formulating, and plastics molding by September 2028.

The bill requires monitoring to begin immediately upon enactment for the regulated industries, plus pulp and paper mills, airports, and electrical components makers, with EPA deciding by the end of 2026 whether those additional categories also get discharge limits.

Publicly owned treatment works would receive $200 million per year through 2030 to run pretreatment programs and track local sources of PFAS entering their plants, shifting some cleanup cost from ratepayers to the federal government.
EPA would have to make a standardized PFAS testing method (Method 1633A) official by January 2026, so monitoring results are consistent and enforceable nationwide.

analysis.who_pays: The industries that discharge PFAS — plastics and synthetic fibers makers, electroplating and metal finishing shops, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint makers, and plastics molders — would bear the cost of monitoring, testing, and installing treatment to meet new discharge limits. Taxpayers would fund the $200 million a year in treatment-works grants and $12 million a year for EPA's work, subject to annual appropriations. Some costs would likely reach consumers through prices on PFAS-dependent goods.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on manufacturers, landfills, and other dischargers, and some of those costs would be passed to consumers through higher prices for goods like textiles, coatings, and metal products.

The $200 million a year in grants for sewage plants is only an authorization, not an actual appropriation, so Congress could fund it at zero and leave treatment plants facing PFAS pretreatment duties without federal help.
The bill sets rigid statutory deadlines for EPA rulemaking across many industries at once, which could strain the agency's capacity and invite legal challenges over deadlines that prove unrealistic.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is large and the deadline structure is unusually specific, which makes the bill more enforceable than a typical directive to EPA. The main weaknesses are that the grant funding depends on future appropriations and that the compliance burden lands on a broad set of industries on a fast timeline. On balance, the benefits of reducing PFAS in water — a chemical linked to serious health harms — outweigh the costs, though the bill's fate depends entirely on whether Congress ever advances it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in December 2025 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no action.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on December 11, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The bill lists zero cosponsors, and no committee hearing, markup, or floor action has occurred since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the industries that discharge PFAS are better off, since the enforceable discharge limits and mandatory monitoring the bill would impose have not moved, and EPA faces no statutory deadlines from it.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee; recruited no cosponsors in the record shown.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since it was referred in December 2025.

sides.party_line_note: No other senator has joined the bill and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is unknown.

industries.industry: Chemicals, plastics, and synthetic fibers manufacturers
industries.note: First in line for mandatory PFAS discharge limits by September 2026 plus immediate monitoring. Their discharge costs rise, but the public gains cleaner water.
Face PFAS monitoring starting immediately and enforceable discharge limits by September 2026, requiring new testing and treatment equipment.
Textiles are a major PFAS use; the industry would face monitoring now and discharge limits by September 2027.
Landfill leachate is a major PFAS pathway into water; the bill imposes monitoring now and discharge limits by September 2027.

industries.industry: Leather tanning, paint, and plastics molding industries
industries.note: Would face monitoring immediately and PFAS discharge limits by September 2028.
The bill sends them $200 million a year to run PFAS pretreatment programs, shifting cleanup costs off local ratepayers.

industries.industry: Airports, pulp and paper mills, and electronics makers
industries.note: They would face immediate PFAS monitoring costs, but EPA could decline to set discharge limits for them after a 2026 review.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the profile of one that dies quietly: a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since its December 2025 referral. Barring a push for cosponsors, a committee hearing, or attachment to a larger water or infrastructure package, it is likely to sit in the Environment and Public Works Committee until this Congress ends in January 2027.
